cap: After evacuation of a mole, hCG should fall to undetectable. Four values within 10 percent over 3 weeks, a rise of more than 10 percent over 2 weeks, or hCG still detectable at 6 months defines gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is staged and scored. A score of 6 or less is cured with single-agent chemotherapy, 7 or more needs multiagent treatment, and placental site tumors need hysterectomy.
teach: The plateau or rise criteria look at serial values, not one number, so every patient has weekly hCG until it is undetectable. FIGO stage runs from I, confined to the uterus, to IV, other sites such as brain and liver; stage III is lung. The WHO score adds points for age, the antecedent pregnancy (mole scores lowest), months since it, pretreatment hCG, tumor size, number and site of metastases and prior failed chemotherapy. Choriocarcinoma spreads by blood to the lungs first, so a chest film belongs in every work-up, and metastases are not biopsied because they bleed. Placental site and epithelioid trophoblastic tumors arise from intermediate trophoblast, make little hCG, and are chemoresistant, so hysterectomy treats localized disease.
